subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The $75,000 Threshold
description: A short lesson to help you apply The $75,000 Threshold.

hook.text: Kahneman found happiness rises with income up to $75,000 a year. After that, more money didn't add more daily happiness.

buildup.text: Below the threshold, money reduces stress from bills, rent, and basic needs. Above it, diminishing returns kick in hard.

discovery.text: Killingsworth later found that happiness does keep rising above $75k, but the rate flattens.

twist.text: The exception: people who are unhappy see no benefit above $100k. For them, money doesn't fix what cash can't buy.

climax.text: Money solves money problems. Once those are solved, purpose, relationships, and autonomy drive happiness.

punchline.text: Enough money buys freedom. More money buys stuff.

quiz.question: What did research find about income and happiness?
options: More money always means more happiness
Happiness rises with income but with diminishing returns above a threshold
Money has no relationship to happiness

details.summary: A landmark study found that emotional wellbeing increases with income up to about $75,000 per year, after which additional income shows diminishing returns for daily happiness. More recent research suggests the relationship may continue but flatten significantly.
details.whyItMatters: The $75,000 threshold challenged the assumption that more money always equals more happiness. It reframes the pursuit of income beyond a comfort level as yielding diminishing emotional returns compared to other investments in wellbeing.
takeaways: Income strongly affects happiness below the threshold of basic financial security
Above the threshold, additional income has diminishing emotional returns
Recent research by Killingsworth suggests some relationship continues beyond $75K

faq.question: Is the $75,000 figure still accurate today?
faq.answer: The exact number varies by location and should be adjusted for inflation. Updated research by Matthew Killingsworth suggests wellbeing continues to rise with income beyond $75K, though at a decreasing rate. The core insight about diminishing returns remains valid.

faq.question: Why does money stop buying happiness after a certain point?
faq.answer: Below the threshold, money solves problems that cause daily distress: food insecurity, unpaid bills, lack of healthcare. Above it, basic needs are met and additional income goes to luxuries that are subject to rapid hedonic adaptation.
